title: Conclusion
text:
What the team should do

Set checkout ETAs by origin/destination state and month, not one flat average. Geography and purchase month alone (LM on Recipe 2, 7.889 days RMSE, \(R^2 = 0.246\)) capture almost all of the baseline gain over a simple numeric model (LM on Recipe 1, 8.872 days RMSE, \(R^2 = 0.046\)).
Use Ridge (Recipe 3) as the baseline ETA model. It edges out LM (Recipe 2), Lasso (Recipe 3) (7.891 days RMSE, 5.243 days MAE), and Decision Tree (Recipe 4) (7.937 days RMSE, 5.222 days MAE) on test RMSE and \(R^2\) while keeping predictions smooth across correlated numeric features (freight_value and product_weight_g).
Add an upper buffer window for long-haul and tail-risk orders. Because point predictions cluster around typical delivery windows (~5–25 days), extreme delays past 50–150+ days still produce large positive residuals (Actual - Predicted > 0). Pairing the point estimate with a delivery window helps manage expectations on slower routes.
Group low-volume states cleanly in baseline models. Using step_other(threshold = 0.02) prevents noisy estimates on small state samples in the training set while preserving signal from major and distinct regional patterns.

title: Conclusion
text:
How far to trust it
-Around 5.22 days MAE and **7.86 days RMSE on unseen test orders—useful for checkout ETA windows and capacity planning, but not exact to the single day on every shipment.
-Tail delays are still the hardest part: Residuals are skewed upward on extreme outliers where deliveries stretch far beyond typical transit times, so point estimates will under-predict severe exceptions.
-Random split tests “similar orders,” not future shifts: The 80/20 split (88,156 train / 22,040 test) measures generalization across orders from the historical dataset, not performance under future carrier changes or seasonal shifts.
-Order-item grain carries through: Because delivery_days is an order-level delivery duration repeated across items in multi-item orders (110,196 rows), multi-item orders have slightly more weight in the metrics

text:
Decision, Limitations, and Next Steps (Milestone 2)
Adopt route- and weight-aware delivery buffers rather than a single flat delivery promise—for example, accounting for multi-week differences between SP (8.3 mean customer days) and distant states such as RR (27.8 mean days), as well as heavier 10kg+ shipments (14.9 mean days)
### Limitations Historical scope & missing timestamps: The Olist dataset covers 2016–2018 operations and omits orders lacking recorded delivery dates, so estimates may not reflect current carrier routing or unfulfilled orders. Small counts in remote states & non-predictive outcome fields: Low order counts in remote states increase variance of raw averages, and post-delivery fields (delayed_days, delivered_status) are excluded from feature exploration to avoid leakage.

Why this matters
Olist is a Brazilian online marketplace that connects small sellers to customers across the country. Delivery speed and shipping cost are central to customer satisfaction, and they are set by logistics: where the seller and customer are, how heavy the item is, and what category it belongs to. About two years of order data (2016-2018) can show where the delivery promise holds, where it breaks, and what drives shipping costs.

What I found so far

About 90% of orders arrive earlier than estimated, so Olist’s delivery estimates are conservative.
Purchase timing (weekday vs. weekend, time of day) barely changes delivery outcomes.
Location and product type matter more: delivery time varies by customer state and by category, and heavier items cost more to ship.

Summary of Cleaning Decisions (One Sentence per Rule)

Column name & date standardization: Corrected the raw typos (product_name_lenght -> product_name_length and product_description_lenght -> product_description_length) and built purchase_year_month so naming is consistent and monthly trends can be tracked cleanly.
Missing target removal: Removed 2,454 rows (2.18%) missing delivery_days—moving from 112,650 to 110,196 rows—because records without an observed delivery duration cannot train or evaluate a delivery_days model.
Category missingness ("unknown"): Filled missing product_category_name and product_category_name_english entries with "unknown" rather than dropping rows so uncategorized items still contribute shipping, timing, and geographic records.
Numeric product spec imputation (median): Imputed missing values across the seven numeric product specification columns (product_name_length, product_description_length, product_photos_qty, product_weight_g, product_length_cm, product_height_cm, and product_width_cm) using each column’s median because product dimensions and counts are skewed and the median resists extreme outliers.

title: Modeling
text:
This page builds straightforward baseline models to predict delivery_days (days from order purchase to customer delivery) using the cleaned dataset (data/df_master_clean.rds) from data.qmd[cite: 2, 3]. Following the tidymodels workflow from Weeks 8–12, we check target skewness first, split into training and testing sets, inspect numeric correlations and categorical groups on the training set, define four recipes, fit linear regression, Lasso, Ridge, and decision tree models, compare them against a naive baseline on the test set, and inspect diagnostic plots[cite: 3].
Post-delivery or target-derived fields (such as delayed_days or delivered_status) are excluded from predictors, and all preprocessing steps (step_other(), step_dummy(), step_normalize()) are learned inside workflows fitted only on the training set[cite: 2].

library(tidymodels)
library(corrplot)
library(rpart.plot)
library(knitr)

  mutate(

    product_category_name_english = factor(product_category_name_english)
